Nonlinear transcriptional responses to gradual modulation
of transcription factor dosage
4

13 * Corresponding authors: jdomingo@nygenome.org; tlappalainen@nygenome.org
✝ Current affiliation: Allostery Exploration Technologies, S.L., Barcelona, Spain.

Abstract
Genomic loci associated with common traits and diseases are typically non-coding and likely 18 impact gene expression, sometimes coinciding with rare loss-of-function variants in the 19 target gene. However, our understanding of how gradual changes in gene dosage affect 20 molecular, cellular, and organismal traits is currently limited. To address this gap, we 21 induced gradual changes in gene expression of four genes using CRISPR activation and 22 inactivation. Downstream transcriptional consequences of dosage modulation of three 23 master trans-regulators associated with blood cell traits (GFI1B, NFE2, and MYB) were 24 examined using targeted single-cell multimodal sequencing. We showed that guide tiling 25 around the TSS is the most effective way to modulate cis gene expression across a wide 26 range of fold-changes, with further effects from chromatin accessibility and histone marks 27 that differ between the inhibition and activation systems. Our single-cell data allowed us to 28 precisely detect subtle to large gene expression changes in dozens of trans genes, revealing 29 that many responses to dosage changes of these three TFs are nonlinear, including non30 monotonic behaviours, even when constraining the fold-changes of the master regulators to 31 a copy number gain or loss. We found that the dosage properties are linked to gene 32 constraint and that some of these nonlinear responses are enriched for disease and GWAS 33 genes. Overall, our study provides a straightforward and scalable method to precisely 34 modulate gene expression and gain insights into its downstream consequences at high 35 resolution.
Introduction
38 Precision control of gene expression levels plays a pivotal role in defining cell type specificity 39 and coordinating responses to external stimuli. Imbalances in this intricate regulation can
available under a CC-BY 4.0 International license.
(which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder, who has granted bioRxiv a license to display the preprint in perpetuity. It is made


underlie the genetic basis of both common and rare human diseases. The vast majority of 41 genetic variants associated with complex disease, as revealed by genome-wide association 42 studies (GWAS), are located in noncoding regions, with likely gene regulatory effects 1. 43 Previous studies have attempted to elucidate these effects by mapping genetic associations 44 to gene expression 2,3, and more recently, CRISPR-based perturbations of GWAS loci have 45 provided insights into their functional consequences 4. A major driver of rare genetic 46 diseases is loss-of-function variants affecting one or both copies of the gene, leading to 47 disease via dramatic reduction of functional gene dosage 5. The substantial overlap 6,7 and 48 potential joint effects 8,9 of rare and common variants indicate a general link between 49 different degrees of perturbation of gene dosage and disease phenotypes. 50 51 However, our understanding of the quantitative relationship between gradual changes in 52 gene dosage and downstream phenotypes remains elusive for most human genes. Practical 53 applications of the compelling allelic series concept to identify genes where increasingly 54 deleterious mutations have increasing phenotypic effects have been limited by the sparsity 55 of segregating variants with an impact on a given gene in the human population 10. 56 Experimental characterization of gene function in model systems has predominantly relied 57 on gene knock-out or knock-down approaches 11. While these studies have proven useful to 58 identify dosage-sensitive genes involved in cellular functions and disease 12–16, these 59 approaches only provide a limited discrete relationship between the number of functional 60 gene copies and a certain phenotype (eg. loss-of-function consequence vs. wild-type). 61 However, such relationships are in fact determined by continuous dosage-to-phenotypes 62 functions that, as suggested by a small number of previous experimental studies 17–19, can 63 be complex and thus are challenging to infer from loss-/gain-of-function data. 64 65 Recently, new methods have enabled the gradual modulation of gene dosage in model 66 systems 18,20–22, while large-scale insights into the downstream effects of dosage modulation 67 have largely come from yeast 17 and bacteria 19,23, demonstrating that nonlinear relationships 68 between gene dosage and phenotype are common. In humans, the relationship between dosage and downstream phenotypes is largely unexplored. Only a few limited studies 17–19
70 have dissected these consequences. For instance, the disease-associated transcription 71 factor SOX9 24 showed a nonlinear relationship between dosage and multiple tiers of 72 phenotypes, including DNA accessibility, RNA expression of downstream targets, raising 73 the question of whether this phenomenon occurs with other transcription factors. More 74 recently, similar evidence has been shown in the case of the NKX2-1 lineage factor with an 75 oncogenic role in lung adenocarcinoma 25. Generally, transcription factors represent a 76 particularly compelling target for the characterization of gene dosage effects. They are key 77 regulators of cellular functions, enriched for disease associations 26 and often classified as 78 haploinsufficient 27. Additionally, their effects can be measured by transcriptome analysis. 79 However, our knowledge of their dosage-dependent effects on regulatory networks still 80 remains limited, particularly regarding subtle dosage variation within their natural range 22. 81 82 In this study, we developed and characterised a scalable novel sgRNA design approach for 83 gradually decreasing and increasing gene dosage with the CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) 84 and activation (CRISPRa) systems. We applied this to four genes, with single-cell RNA85 sequencing (scRNA-seq) as a cellular readout of downstream effects. While classic Perturb86 Seq analyses have focused on gene knockdown effects, we assess the effects of gradual 87 up- and down-regulation of target genes. We uncovered quantitative patterns of how gradual

(which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder, who has granted bioRxiv a license to display the preprint in perpetuity. It is made


changes in transcription dosage lead to linear and nonlinear responses in downstream 89 genes. Many downstream genes are associated with rare and complex diseases, with 90 potential effects on cellular phenotypes.
Results
Precise modulation and quantification of gene dosage using
CRISPR and targeted multimodal single-cell sequencing
95 We selected four genes for gradual modulation of their dosage in the human erythroid 96 progenitor cell line K562 28: GFI1B, NFE2, MYB and TET2. Two of the genes, GFI1B and 97 NFE2, have been implicated in blood diseases and traits 29–31, and in our earlier work, we 98 identified a broad transcriptional response to inhibition of GWAS-overlapping enhancers to 99 these genes 4. MYB is a key transcription factor 32 and a downstream target of GFI1B 4.TET2 100 has a role in DNA demethylation and is unrelated to these transcriptional networks and is 101 included in this study as a control with minimal expected trans effects. We refer to these four 102 genes, targeted in cis for modulation of their regulation, as cis genes (Figure 1A). 103 104 To modulate the gene expression of the cis genes, we use K562 cells expressing CRISPRi 105 (KRAB-dCas9-MECP2) and CRISPRa (dCas9-VPR) systems (see Methods), both cell lines 106 were hashed with DNA conjugated antibodies against different surface proteins that allow 107 pooled experiments. To obtain a wide range of dosage effects we used four different single 108 guide RNA (sgRNA) design strategies (Figure 1B): 1) targeting the transcription start site 109 (TSS) as in the standard CRISPRi/CRISPRa approach, 2) tiling sgRNAs +/- 1000 bp from 110 the TSS in approximately 100bp intervals, 3) targeting known cis-regulatory elements 111 (CREs), and 4) using attenuated guides that target the TSS but contain mismatches to 112 modulate their activity 18. We further included 5 non-targeting control (NTC) sgRNAs as 113 negative controls. 114 115 The library of altogether 96 guides was transduced to a pool of K562-CRISPRi and K562116 CRISPRa cells at low multiplicity of infection (MOI). After eight days, we performed ECCITE117 seq (see Methods) to capture three modalities: cDNA, sgRNAs and surface protein hashes 118 (oligo-tagged antibodies with unique barcodes against ubiquitously expressed surface 119 proteins). Instead of sequencing the full transcriptome, we used target hybridization to 120 capture a smaller fraction of the cDNA and obtain more accurate expression readouts at a 121 feasible cost. The subset of selected transcripts were picked from the transcriptional 122 downstream regulatory networks of GFI1B and NFE2 identified previously 4, maintaining 123 similar patterns of co-expression correlation across co-expression clusters (see Methods, 124 Figure S1A). We targeted a total of 94 transcripts (Figure 1A), including the four cis genes, 125 86 genes that represent trans targets of GFI1B and/or NFE2 4 (Figure S1A), LXH3 that is 126 not expressed in blood progenitors, GAPDH that is highly expressed and often considered 127 an invariable housekeeping gene and the dCas9-VPR or KRAB-dCas9-MeCP2 transcripts. 128 129 We used the protein hashes and the dCas9 cDNA (indicating the presence or absence of the 130 KRAB domain) to demultiplex and determine the cell line—CRISPRi or CRISPRa. Cells
available under a CC-BY 4.0 International license.
(which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder, who has granted bioRxiv a license to display the preprint in perpetuity. It is made


containing a single sgRNA were identified using a Gaussian mixture model (see Methods). 132 Standard quality control procedures were applied to the scRNA-seq data (see Methods). To 133 confirm that the targeted transcript capture approach worked as intended, we assessed 134 concordance across capture lanes (Figure S1C). The final data set had 20,001 cells (10,647 135 CRISPRi and 9,354 CRISPRa), with an average of 81 and 86 cells with a unique sgRNA for 136 the CRISPRa and CRISPRi, respectively (Figure S1D). 137
Gradual modulation of gene expression across a broad range
with CRISPRi/a
141 Next, we calculated the expression fold change for each of the four cis genes targeted by 142 each sgRNA in the two cell lines (CRISPRi/a), comparing each group of cells with its 143 respective NTC sgRNA group (see Methods). We first confirmed that the sgRNAs targeting 144 the transcription start site (TSS) up- and down-regulated their targets (Figure 1C, Figure 145 S1F). When looking at all sgRNAs at once, across the four genes, we observed a 2.3 fold 146 range (Figure 1E), with a minimum 72% reduction and maximum 174% increased 147 expression (log2(FC) values from -1.83 to 0.80). However, the range varied between the 148 genes, with GFI1B covering the widest range of gene expression changes (gene expression 149 ranging between 0.28 to 1.42 fold), while MYB expression could not be pushed higher than 150 1.13 fold (Figure 1E). The direction of the effects were consistent with the cell lines of origin, 151 where 98.88% of the significant perturbations (Wilcoxon rank test at 10% FDR, n = 89) were 152 correctly predicted based on the direction of the target gene fold change. The predicted on153 and off-target properties of the guides 33–35 did not correlate with the fold changes in the cis 154 genes (Figure S2A), suggesting that the observed effects represent true cis-regulatory 155 changes. The fold changes were also robust to the number of cells containing a particular 156 sgRNA (Figure S2B, top). 157 158 We verified that the fold change estimation was not biased depending on the expression 159 level of the target gene at the single-cell level, which can vary due to drop-out effects or 160 binary on/off effects of the KRAB-based CRISPRi system 20. By splitting cells with the same 161 sgRNA based on the normalised expression of the cis gene (0 vs. >0 normalised UMIs, 162 Figure S3A), we observed highly concordant transcriptome gene expression effects 163 between the two groups (Figure S3B). This indicates that the dosage changes per guide 164 were not primarily driven by the changing frequency of binary on/off effects, and the use of 165 pseudo-bulk fold changes provides a robust estimation of cis gene fold changes. These 166 patterns are further supported by the cells forming a gradient rather than distinct clusters on 167 a UMAP (Figure S3C). 168 169 The fold change patterns differed between sgRNA designs (Figure 1D, left). As expected, 170 sgRNAs targeting the TSS showed strong perturbations in gene expression. However, 171 sgRNAs tiled +/- 1kb from the TSS provided a broader and more gradual range of up- and 172 downregulation across the target genes, sometimes surpassing the effects of TSS-targeting 173 sgRNAs. Attenuated sgRNAs with mismatch mutations resulted in a range of gene silencing 174 effects in the CRISPRi line, as expected based on their original design 18. However, these 175 attenuated sgRNAs did not exhibit such a dynamic range in the CRISPRa modality, although
available under a CC-BY 4.0 International license.
(which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder, who has granted bioRxiv a license to display the preprint in perpetuity. It is made


a significant correlation existed between the silencing or activating effect size and the 177 distance of the mismatch from the protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) when considering all 178 data points together (Figure S2C). The sgRNAs targeting distal cis-regulatory elements 179 (CREs) showed both inhibiting and activating effects, even though both the CRISPRi and 180 CRISPRa constructs were initially designed to inhibit or activate transcription from the 181 promoter and initial gene body region. Nonetheless, the number of known CREs per gene is 182 typically limited. Given its simplicity and the ability to achieve both up- and downregulation of 183 the target gene, we consider the tiling sgRNA approach, with a simple design that only 184 requires annotation of the TSS, as a useful method for gradually modulating gene dosage 185 with CRISPRi/a systems.
Cis determinants of dosage
188 Having designed guides targeting both distal and local neighbouring regulatory regions of 189 the four transcription factors (TFs) and ensuring minimal bias in fold-changes due to 190 sgRNA’s biochemical properties, we investigated the cis features that determine the strength 191 of dosage perturbation. We observed substantial differences in the effects of the same guide 192 on the CRISPRi and CRISPRa backgrounds, with no significant correlation between cis 193 gene fold-changes (Figure 2A). However, in both modalities, the strongest effects on gene 194 expression were observed when the guides were close to the transcription start site (TSS) 195 (Figure 2B, excluding NTC and attenuated sgRNAs), although the peaks of strongest 196 activation or repression differed between the modalities. In the CRISPRi modality, the 197 maximum effect was located within the gene body at +238 bp from the TSS (Figure 2B, 198 bottom), consistent with previous studies that used essentiality as a proxy for expression 36. 199 However, in the CRISPRa modality, the maximum average fold changes occurred closer to 200 the TSS at around -99 bp (Figure 2B, bottom), as also shown for CD45 37. 201 202 Enhancer, tiling, and TSS sgRNAs targeted regions of the genome with different 203 compositions of histone marks, annotated by ENCODE, in K562 cells38 (Figure 2C), which 204 allowed us to investigate the impact of chromatin state on the strength of cis gene dosage 205 modulation. The magnitude of cis gene fold changes varied significantly depending on the 206 presence of specific marks or peaks, which again differed between the two modalities 207 (Figure 2D). In the CRISPRa cell line, the strongest effects were observed when guides 208 were located in regions with open chromatin marks, such as DNase or ATAC peaks. In 209 contrast, the strongest repression by CRISPRi occurred in genomic regions with the 210 presence of H3K27ac, H3K4me3, and H3K9ac marks. These differences may be explained 211 by the distinct mechanisms of action of the activator and repressor domains. MeCP2 and 212 KRAB repressor domains recruit additional repressors that silence gene expression through 213 chromatin remodelling activities such as histone deacetylation 39. On the other hand, the 214 VPR activation fusion domain may only require Cas9 to scan the open chromatin and recruit 215 RNA polymerase and additional transcription factors to activate transcription. Overall, while a 216 few sgRNAs have a strong effect in both CRISPRi and CRISPRa cell lines, a single guide 217 library containing guides optimised for both modalities enables a range of gradual dosage 218 regulation. However, larger data sets are needed for more careful modelling of the ideal 219 dosage modulation designs and to understand how both cis-regulatory features, feedback 220 loops, and other mechanisms contribute to the outcomes.

Trans responses of transcription factor dosage modulation
223 We then turned our attention to the remaining 91 genes captured by our custom panel and 224 determined the relative expression fold change of each trans gene, compared to NTC in 225 each unique guide perturbation (see Methods). Principal component analysis (PCA) 226 performed on all pseudo-bulk fold changes demonstrated the removal of batch effects from 227 the cell lines and revealed a clear direction of the cis gene dosage effect in the first three 228 principal components (Figure S4B). This finding suggests that dosage modulation is the 229 primary determinant of trans effects. The PCA indicated that the dosage modulation of 230 GFI1B and MYB is reflected in opposite directions in PC1 and PC2, while the trans 231 responses of NFE2 are captured by PC3. 232 233 Using a false discovery rate (FDR) cutoff of 0.05, all 91 trans genes except for the neural234 specific TF LHX3 (negative control) exhibited a significant change in expression upon 235 perturbation of any of the TFs. The observed trans-effects were well correlated with 236 perturbations of these genes in other data sets (Figure S4C,D). Among all measured fold 237 changes, the most extreme negative effect sizes were observed in cis genes, with the top 10 238 being predominantly reductions in GFI1B expression. This indicates that cis downregulation 239 tended to surpass the endogenous expression limits. In contrast, the largest increases in 240 gene expression were observed through trans mechanisms, where KLK1 and TUBB1 241 reached the largest expression values when GFI1B was strongly upregulated, or SPI1 and 242 DAPK1 when GFI1B was strongly downregulated. These findings suggest that the CRISPRa 243 approach did not reach a biological ceiling of overexpression. 244 245 Inspecting trans responses as a function of cis gene modulation, we observed that the 246 number of expressed genes and the mean absolute expression changes of trans genes 247 exhibited gene-specific correlations with cis-gene dosage (Figure 3A, Figure S4E). 248 Perturbations in GFI1B led to the most pronounced trans responses, with positive dosage 249 changes resulting in larger effect sizes compared to decreasing TF gene expression, where 250 the effect plateaued. NFE2 exhibited similar patterns but with a smaller magnitude. In the 251 case of MYB, trans responses were observed when decreasing the expression of this TF, 252 but the effects of upregulation are largely unknown as we were unable to increase MYB 253 expression beyond 0.35. As expected, given the unrelatedness of TET2 to the trans network, 254 dosage modulation of this gene had minimal trans effects with the least pronounced trend 255 when compared to TET2 dosage, so we excluded it from subsequent analyses.
Widespread nonlinear dosage responses in trans regulatory
networks
259 Upon clustering the changes in expression of trans genes based on the cis gene dosage 260 change linked to each sgRNA, we identified distinct clusters exhibiting different dosage261 response patterns (Figure 3B for GFI1B, Figure S5-8A for all cis genes). Further 262 examination of the gene expression fold changes for each individual trans gene in relation to 263 the TF fold changes revealed a diverse range of response patterns (Figure 3C, Figure S5264 8B for all cis genes). These responses exhibited both linear and nonlinear forms, including
available under a CC-BY 4.0 International license.
(which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder, who has granted bioRxiv a license to display the preprint in perpetuity. It is made


some instances of non-monotonic gene expression responses for certain trans genes within 266 the GFI1B trans network (e.g., GATA2 in Figure 3C, Figure S9E). 267 268 To accurately characterise the dosage response, we employed both linear and nonlinear 269 modelling approaches (Figure 3D), which allowed us to quantitatively assess the extent of 270 nonlinear responses by comparing the goodness of fit of these models using the Akaike 271 Information Criterion (AIC). For the nonlinear model, we utilised a sigmoid function with four 272 free parameters (Figure 3D, right). These parameters represented the slope at the inflection 273 point (b, indicating the rate of increase or decrease in expression), the minimum and 274 maximum asymptotes (c and d, representing the lower and upper limits of fold change), and 275 the value of cis gene expression at which the inflection point occurs (a). To prevent 276 overfitting, we implemented a 10-fold cross-validation scheme, which yielded reliable 277 predictions on the left-out data (Pearson r = 0.71 to 0.88 for all trans genes in the GFI1B, 278 MYB, and NFE2 networks, Figure S9C). Additionally, the predicted parameter a was centred 279 around zero, as expected since the input data represents relative fold changes (Figure S10). 280 Since a sigmoid function cannot capture non-monotonic responses, we employed a loess 281 regression as an alternative approach for the few genes that exhibited non-monotonic 282 responses (see Methods, Figure S9D, E). For the vast majority of genes, the sigmoid (or 283 loess) fit was remarkably good, partially due to the low level of noise in the targeted scRNA284 seq data. 285
We compared the performance of the linear vs. nonlinear models with the ∆AIC ( 卄〒ぁ〲〨ぅ
286
ぅ ), where a positive ∆AIC means that the sigmoid model captures the variance better in
the dosage response than in the linear model. This showed that most GFI1B-dependent
dosage expression responses are better fit by the sigmoid model (median ∆AIC = 18.7, with
70.4% of all trans genes with a significant response having ∆AIC >2, Figure 3D). The
responses to dosage modulation of MYB and NFE2 were also better captured by the
nonlinearities, but to a lesser extent (0.14 and 3.4 median ∆AIC, with 20.8% and 40.7% of all
trans genes dosage responses having ∆AIC > 2 for MYB and NFE2, respectively, Figure
S9A). The broader range of GFI1B expression modulation, providing more data to detect 295 nonlinear trends, likely contributes to this difference. When ignoring those genes classified 296 as unresponsive (genes that their expression did not change upon the TF modulator, see
Methods), even more responses of the remaining trans genes were better explained by a
sigmoidal model with 83.6%, 26.3% and 63.2% of these having a ∆AIC > 2, for GFI1B, MYB
and NFE2 respectively. A similar trend holds even when limiting the models to be fitted to 300 those data points that correspond to a hypothetical one copy loss or gain of the cis gene
(Figure S9B), where the median ∆AIC of responsive genes are 7.05, 0.05, and 3.6 for
GFI1B, MYB, and NFE2 trans responses. Overall, this shows that trans responses to TF 303 dosage are dominated by nonlinear behaviours even when the TF dosage changes are not 304 extreme but within biologically plausible ranges.

Gene and transcriptional network properties of dosage
response
308 Utilising a model that effectively captures the variance in our data provided the ability to 309 predict unmeasured TF dosage points and facilitated a direct comparison of trans effects 310 across different cis genes. Employing the sigmoid model (and loess for those with non311 monotonic responses), we estimated the continuous expression of trans genes on a uniform 312 fold-change scale across the spectrum of GFI1B, MYB, and NFE2 expression changes 313 (Figure 4A). This estimation was carried out within the empirically observed range of all 314 three cis genes, spanning from log2(FC) -1.83 to 0.51. Subsequent hierarchical clustering of 315 trans gene responses revealed six major clusters of distinct response patterns. For the 316 majority of trans genes, the response to GFI1B and MYB was opposite, with only two small 317 clusters displaying exceptions. Notably, GFI1B generally induced the most substantial 318 response, while NFE2 triggered the smallest range of trans gene response. 319 320 Next, we collected diverse annotations for the trans genes to explore the connections 321 between their regulatory properties, disease associations, and selective constraints 322 concerning their response to TF dosage (Figure 4B, C). To quantify these relationships, we 323 assessed significant differences in belonging to these qualitative annotations using the 324 Wilcoxon rank test (Figure 4D) and correlated parameters from the sigmoid model with 325 quantitative gene metrics (Figure 4E). We hypothesised that genes with annotated selective 326 constraint, numerous regulatory elements, and central positions in regulatory networks 327 would exhibit greater robustness to TF changes. Indeed, housekeeping genes demonstrated 328 a considerably smaller dosage response range (Figure 4F). Moreover, genes classified as 329 unresponsive were enriched in the housekeeping category (odds ratio = 2.14, Fisher test p330 value = 0.024). The link between selective constraint and response properties is most 331 apparent in the MYB trans network. Specifically, the probability of haploinsufficiency 332 (pHaplo) shows a significant negative correlation with the dynamic range of transcriptional 333 responses (Figure 4G): genes under stronger constraint (higher pHaplo) display smaller 334 dynamic ranges, indicating that dosage-sensitive genes are more tightly buffered against 335 changes in MYB levels. This pattern was not reproduced in the other trans networks (Figure 336 4E). 337 338 The relationship between the response of trans genes and intrinsic gene properties differed 339 between GFI1B, MYB, and NFE2 trans network responses. We also performed a similar 340 analysis comparing the sigmoid parameters to network properties using the approach 341 outlined by Minaeva et al.40and obtained inconsistent results between TF regulons (Figure 342 S11A, B). This suggests that the link between commonly annotated gene properties and the 343 gene responses are complex and highly context specific, as in our data from a single cell 344 line, they differed between the upstream regulators that were manipulated. Thus, much more 345 data is needed before transcriptional responses can be predicted from gene properties, and 346 conversely, to understand the cellular mechanisms that lead to the annotated gene 347 properties.

Nonlinear dosage responses in complex traits and disease
350 Moving beyond the characterization of mechanisms of transcriptome regulation, a key 351 question is how gradual dosage variation links to downstream cellular phenotypes, and 352 whether these responses exhibit analogous nonlinear patterns. To address this question, we 353 correlated our findings with the expression profiles of various cell types in order to study the 354 myeloid differentiation process, a phenotype well-characterised for our K562 model that has 355 been used as a reliable system for investigating erythroid differentiation within myeloid 356 lineages 41 and blood tumours 42. Specifically, leveraging single-cell expression data for bone 357 marrow cell types from the Human Cell Atlas and Human Biomolecular Atlas Project 43, we 358 filtered the expression data to the targeted genes in our study. After aggregating data across 359 donors and normalising expression across cell types (Figure S12A), we compared the 360 expression patterns resulting from each unique transcription factor dosage modulation in 361 relation to each unique cell type expression state. The ensuing correlation can then be 362 construed as a "phenotype," signifying the similarity between the transcriptional state 363 induced by the TF increase or decrease and the transcriptional state of a specific blood 364 lineage cell type. 365 366 Such analyses recapitulate known biology, with GFI1B upregulation 29 and MYB 367 downregulation 44 being crucial factors promoting erythrocyte maturation (Figure 5A). The 368 downregulation of NFE2 instead was negatively related to platelet differentiation. Analysing 369 the correlations as inferred phenotypes suggests potential nonlinear relationships (Figure 370 S12B), but these trends should be considered hypotheses that require experimental 371 validation. In summary, this points to cellular phenotypes resulting from gradual TF dosage 372 modulation. 373 374 Many of the analysed trans genes are associated with physiological traits and diseases 375 (Figure 4). Understanding the nonlinear trends in the expression of these genes is of 376 particular interest, as it helps comprehend how genes with physiological impacts may be 377 buffered against upstream regulatory changes, and how their dosage changes as a 378 response to upstream regulators contrasts with genetic variants that contribute to diseases 379 and traits. Additionally, knowing the underlying dosage-to-phenotype curve of a gene can be 380 crucial if this is considered a biomarker for identifying or treating disease. To investigate this, 381 we analysed whether OMIM genes for rare diseases and Mendelian traits or GWAS genes 382 for different blood cell traits (Figure 5B) that are part of the trans networks of genes affected 383 by GFI1B, MYB, or NFE2 perturbation are enriched for nonlinear dosage responses. As 384 seen in Figure 4, the trans response properties of each gene are highly specific to the 385 regulators and thus analysed in parallel for each cis gene network. An enrichment for 386 nonlinear responses was observed for MYB trans network genes associated with disease 387 and for blood traits related to white blood cells and reticulocytes. These enrichments are 388 particularly interesting given that most trans genes that were sensitive to MYB dosage 389 modulation did not respond with a nonlinear trend (Figure S9A). 390 391 Despite nonlinear responses not being significantly enriched among disease genes across 392 all trans networks, the responses of the same trans gene can show very different dosage 393 responses depending on the upstream regulator being tuned. In Figure 5C, we highlight 394 several disease-associated genes (linked to one or more disease phenotypes 45. FOXP1, a
available under a CC-BY 4.0 International license.
(which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder, who has granted bioRxiv a license to display the preprint in perpetuity. It is made


395 haploinsufficient and potentially triplosensitive transcription factor implicated in intellectual 396 disability, exhibited a strong and dose-dependent response, particularly to varying levels of 397 GFI1B. A similar pattern was observed for NFIA, another haploinsufficient gene involved in 398 developmental disorders.. However, it is difficult to interpret their expression response in 399 K562 cells when their most apparent phenotypic effects likely derive from other cell types. 400 RHB is the Rhesus blood type gene, where a common deletion of the gene causes the Rh401 blood type in homozygous individuals, with a strong nonlinear response to GFI1B levels. A 402 particularly interesting gene is TUBB1, part of β-tubulin, that causes autosomal dominant 403 macrothrombocytopenia or abnormally large platelets. Here, K562 cells are a reasonable 404 model system, being closely related precursors to megakaryocytes that produce platelets. 405 Interestingly, GFI1B loss also causes a macrothrombocytopenia phenotype in mice 46, and in 406 our data, TUBB1 expression decreases quickly as a function of decreased GFI1B 407 expression but then plateaus at a level that corresponds to loss of one copy of TUBB1. This 408 raises the hypothesis that low GFI1B levels may cause macrothrombocytopenia at least 409 partially via reducing TUBB1 expression.

Discussion
413 In this paper, we have investigated how gradual dosage modulation of transcription factors 414 contributes to dosage-sensitive transcriptional regulation and investigated its potential 415 phenotypic consequences. First, we set up an easily scalable and generalizable 416 CRISPRi/CRISPRa approach with tiling sgRNAs for gradual titration of gene expression, 417 with reagents that can be designed with data only of the TSS and easily ordered at scale. 418 Alternative approaches that rely e.g., on targeting CREs that are often unknown, dramatic 419 overexpression, or laborious setting up of constructs for each gene are less practical for 420 large-scale analyses. Our approach appears best suited for expression modulation in the 421 biologically reasonable range, and other methods would be needed for dramatic 422 overexpression or complete silencing of the target genes. Our inability to substantially 423 increase MYB expression indicates the need for further work and larger cis gene sets to fully 424 understand how widespread this is and to what extent this depends on cis-regulatory 425 properties versus feedback and buffering mechanisms. Nevertheless, we believe that the 426 approach proposed here is a useful complement to the diversifying set of tools for dosage 427 modulation for different purposes 18–22. 428 429 In this work, we made use of targeted transcriptome sequencing to avoid complications from 430 the sparsity of single-cell data. While highly accurate targeted readout of the cis gene 431 expression linked to each sgRNA is a core component of our approach, analysing trans 432 responses could also be achieved by standard single-cell sequencing of the full 433 transcriptome, possibly in combination with a targeted readout of transcripts of particular 434 interest. In this study, the targeted genes were selected based on prior data of responding to 435 GFI1B, NFE2, or MYB regulation and thus do not represent an unbiased or random sample 436 of genes. An interesting future extension would be the addition of single-cell protein 437 quantification to confirm that the detected mRNA levels correspond to protein levels, but this 438 remains technically challenging. 439 440 Our results show that nonlinear responses to gradual up- and down-regulation of TF dosage 441 are widespread and can be detected even without extreme overexpression or full knockout 442 of the TF. The patterns of transcriptional responses are highly context-specific and vary 443 between upstream regulators. Further work with larger sets of cis and trans genes, as well 444 as direct quantification of cellular readouts, will be needed to fully characterise the patterns 445 and mechanisms of downstream impacts on gene dosage. However, our findings indicate 446 important directions for future research. First, the widespread nonlinearity suggests that 447 inferring gene function from classical molecular biology approaches—such as drastic 448 knockouts or knockdowns—may be limited, as these perturbations can produce effects that 449 are both quantitatively and qualitatively different from the more modest changes that occur 450 naturally. This may be particularly relevant for essential and highly dosage-sensitive genes, 451 where applying our gradual dosage modulation framework can provide opportunities for 452 functional characterization at perturbation levels that do not kill the cells. Secondly, we show 453 that the effects of up- and downregulation are qualitatively and quantitatively different, which 454 calls for increased attention to analysing both directions of effect, which also occur in natural 455 responses to genetic variants and environmental stimuli. 456

Gene dosage sensitivity has typically been studied by human genetics and genomics 458 methods 47–49. The experimental approach pursued in this study and the computational 459 approaches are fundamentally different and complement each other: while human genetics 460 is powerful for capturing the functional importance of physiological phenotypes via patterns 461 of population variation and selective constraint, experimental approaches provide more 462 granularity and insights into cellular mechanisms. Furthermore, while the convergence of 463 disease effects of common and rare variants affecting the same gene is a well-known 464 phenomenon 6,7, the sparsity of variants makes it difficult to properly model allelic series as a 465 continuous dosage-to-phenotype function for individual genes. Experimental approaches can 466 provide a powerful complement to this. Altogether, we envision that combining these 467 perspectives into true systems genetics approaches will be a powerful way to understand 468 how gene dosage variation contributes to human phenotypes from molecular to cellular and 469 eventually physiological levels. 470
